name: uriparser
baseline: Ruby standard library URI.parse (pure Ruby, Ruby 2.6); measured through the ruby-uriparser binding, not through uriparser's C API
workload: 100,000 URI.parse-equivalent calls in a Ruby script (Benchmark.bmbm): a 'complex' URL https://www.ruby-lang.org/en/?a=1#test and a 'simple' URL https://www.ruby-lang.org/en/, Ruby URI vs the UriParser gem (a wrapper around the uriparser C library) vs Addressable.
claimed_speedup: README headline: 'approximatelly 7.5x faster than the standard ruby URI library'. Table, 100,000 parses, measured (non-rehearsal) pass, complex URLs: URI 1.138771 s total (1.215291 real) vs UriParser 0.207083 s total (0.259723 real), about 5.5x on total and 4.7x on real (derived from page data); simple URLs: URI 0.710042 s (0.763542 real) vs UriParser 0.157204 s (0.170975 real), about 4.5x on both (derived from page data). Rehearsal pass complex URLs: 1.146867 s vs 0.156927 s, about 7.3x (derived from page data). Addressable: 2.413826 s (complex), 1.888074 s (simple).
hardware: Mac OS X 10.15.6, 2.7 GHz Dual-Core Intel Core i5, 16 GB 1867 MHz DDR3 (per the wrapper README); Ruby 2.6; C extension compiler and flags not stated
tradeoffs: Strictly RFC 3986 compliant (not WHATWG URL), C99, supports char and wchar_t builds; library is BSD-3-Clause, but the test suite is LGPL-2.1-or-later and the fuzzing code Apache-2.0 (per the README).
caveats: Weak evidence for the uriparser C library itself. The only numbers found are from a third-party Ruby binding (tlewin/ruby-uriparser, MIT, 4 stars, last commit 2021-03-25) timing a C parse against the pure-Ruby stdlib, so the gap is mostly compiled C versus interpreted Ruby and says nothing about uriparser against any C or C++ URI parser (Ada, Boost.URL, curl, Poco, QUrl). The wrapper may also do less work per call than URI.parse (component extraction behaviour not checked). The 7.5x headline does not match the README's own table (4.5x-5.5x on the measured pass; 7.3x only on the rehearsal pass for complex URLs). The simple-URL row times Kernel#URI(...) for the Ruby baseline vs UriParser.parse. README says 100,000 calls while benchmark/benchmark.rb defaults to 10,000 unless an argument is passed. Single run, one machine. uriparser's own README says only 'fast' with no numbers; its ChangeLog, GOALS.txt and repo tree hold no benchmark. A web search for ada-url and Boost.URL benchmarks turned up none that include uriparser (search snippets only). A previous pass (w3-mine-h) filed uriparser as no evidence; this record exists only because of the wrapper's table, and a verifier may reasonably treat it as a binding of the listed project (duplicate) or reject it as not comparable.

name: wepoll
baseline: Winsock select() as used by the JDK's legacy select-based Windows Selector (WindowsSelectorImpl); measured through the JDK NIO Selector, not wepoll against raw select()/WSAPoll in C
workload: OpenJDK JMH microbenchmark SelectOne.testSelectOne: time per Selector.select() call with N loopback SocketChannels registered for OP_READ and one of them ready, N = 1, 10, 100, 1000, 10000; JDK 17 wepoll-based Selector vs the pre-existing select()-based Selector, on Windows Server 2019.
claimed_speedup: wepoll-based Selector vs select-based Selector, ns/op: 1 channel 1428.914 vs 1587.429 (about 1.1x); 10 channels 1429.806 vs 2515.324 (about 1.8x); 100 channels 1433.371 vs 10903.445 (about 7.6x); 1000 channels 1435.007 vs 101651.369 (about 71x); 10000 channels 1445.201 vs 932032.385 (about 645x) (ratios derived from page data). wepoll-based cost stays flat at about 1.43-1.45 us from 1 to 10,000 registered channels while the select-based cost grows linearly. The PR author states the benefit as selection cost depending on ready sockets rather than registered channels.
hardware: Windows Server 2019; CPU model and JDK build not stated on the PR page
stars_or_usage: 1.1k stars; vendored in OpenJDK's Windows Selector since JDK 17 (JDK-8266369, PR 3816 integrated 2021-05-08)
tradeoffs: Windows only (Vista or later), sockets only; level-triggered and one-shot modes, no EPOLLET or EPOLLEXCLUSIVE; epoll port is a HANDLE, not a file descriptor; distributed as a single wepoll.c plus wepoll.h; builds with MSVC, Clang and GCC. The JDK PR text describes it as wrapping the Ancillary Function Driver for Winsock behind an epoll-like interface.
caveats: The only numbers are third-party and indirect. They come from an OpenJDK maintainer's JMH run of the JDK Selector built on wepoll, so the roughly 1.4 us floor includes JVM/JNI and Selector overhead, and the gain at 1 channel is only about 1.1x. The baseline is the JDK's own select() Selector, not WSAPoll, IOCP, or raw select() in C. One ready socket only; the PR notes an exception (select after wakeup) where the old Selector skips selection and gives no number. CPU model and JDK build flags are not stated, and the PR lists 20 iterations while the current benchmark file in openjdk/jdk (test/micro/.../SelectOne.java) uses @Fork(3) with 5 warmup and 5 measurement iterations, so rerunning would use different settings. wepoll's own README makes only qualitative claims ('fast and scalable', 'can poll 100000s of sockets efficiently') with no numbers. No commits since 2020-11-30 (the maintenance status follows the over-3-years rule; the library is stable and still vendored by others).
